text:
Gray and chilly to start this Saturday, 37 and cloudy, and it mostly stays that way. Rain and snow showers get going by late morning and peak between about 2 and 6 this afternoon, with a high near 42. Not much should stick. We're talking about a tenth of an inch of moisture, and any wet snow or bit of graupel will melt on contact in town. Tonight the showers linger until about 10 with a low of 32, so the mix leans a little snowier after dark, but nothing that lasts.

Sunday is the calmer version: mostly cloudy, a high near 42, and a few leftover sprinkles or flurries until mid-morning. The European model is wetter than the forecasters on that, so I'd keep a jacket handy. After that the pattern flips. It turns dry Monday, and by Tuesday we start climbing toward the 50s for much of the week.

For today, grab the umbrella and a warm layer. Sunday afternoon is your better window for a walk.

AFD DISCUSSION (the forecaster's full reasoning, same regional caveat; their temps are area-wide ranges):
KEY MESSAGE 1: Cyclonic northwest flow will prevail under an upper- level low this weekend. A potent embedded shortwave will pass south today and tonight, bringing widespread showers. While they will be most concentrated in the typical northwest flow upslope areas, very marginal instability will develop in the lowest 10,000 ft in the atmosphere due to cold air aloft and solar heating. This will cause the precipitation to trend more convective, especially this afternoon. Therefore, snow showers will be able to survive crossing the terrain and should pass through the downslope areas like the Connecticut River Valley, though likely in a lighter form. While temperatures will rise above freezing below 2,000 ft and likely reach 40 in the lowest points, temperatures will drop significantly in any of the showers. Therefore, even though consistent snow levels will likely only be down to around 1,000-1,500 ft, a period of graupel or even brief wet snow will be possible all the way down into the valleys. However, any continuous accumulations should generally be limited to above 2,000 ft. The showers will gradually become less and less widespread heading into Sunday, and they should be done by Sunday evening. Accumulations by the end should be in the 1-4 inch range above 2,000 ft, with mostly brief coatings that melt below that. The lowest accumulating snow levels will be tonight. Moisture off Lake Champlain will enhance the showers in parts of the Champlain Valley and Greens, but the more convective nature may prevent the formation of distinct bands at times. KEY MESSAGE 2: A potent ridge and associated area of surface high pressure will dominate the weather next week, making it feel as if it were still mid-October. In a classic El Nino pattern, deep troughing and strong surface lows over the Pacific have caused continuous southwest to westerly flow out west, flooding the Great Plains and western Canada with warm Pacific air. This has caused temperature anomalies in the 20-30+ degree range. This airmass will begin to arrive Monday, but clouds will likely remain stuck under the inversion, so it will likely take until Tuesday to warm up. From then through the end of the week, and potentially through the weekend, highs in the 50s will prevail, though 60 will be possible in some of the warmest areas. There will be a strong, persistent subsidence inversion, and it will aided by the fact that significantly more surface heat will be lost at night than will be able to be replenished by the sun during the day. Radiational cooling will help lows drop to the 20s and 30s, around climatological normals. Weak troughs will gradually erode the ridge from the north, but it will take until at least next weekend for it to get pushed to the south and east and for cooler conditions and chances for precipitation to return.

WCAX METEOROLOGIST (regional station — Burlington relevance only, never their branding): BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) - Additional mountain snow is likely today as a compact system moves into our region from Canada. The valleys will have mainly showers and the mountains will have snow showers. Highs will be in the upper 30s to low 40s. This activity will taper to mountain flurries overnight. For Sunday, only scattered valley sprinkles and mountain flurries are expected with minimal accumulation. Total accumulation for this event will be little to nothing in the valleys, and 1 to 3 inches in the mountains, though isolated amounts of 4 to 5 inches can’t be ruled out at the summits. Most of this will occur today. Some higher-elevation roads may become slippery, but impacts will be minor. Next week will have a return to dry weather along with warmer temperatures, so any snow that falls or has fallen will melt. Monday will be partly sunny with highs in the 40s. Lows will be in the 20s to low 30s. Tuesday through Thursday will have plenty of sunshine. Highs will be in the 40s on Tuesday, then some 50s are likely for Wednesday and especially Thursday. With mainly clear skies at night, lows will quickly drop into the 30s each night. Friday will be dry and a touch cooler, but still pleasant, with highs in the upper 40s to low 50s.

Snow accumulation is expected in the northern mountains over the weekend. Drier and brighter weather is likely next week, followed by a warmup into the 50s for several days in a row. That pattern likely continues into at least the beginning of Thanksgiving week.
